findings.title: A declared head launders the tool it runs, and the named limit omits that member
findings.recommendation: The inventory reads only a segment's first token after assignments, and `command`, `sh` and `node` are declared utilities. So `command jq -r .x` reads the head `command` and passes, `sh -c 'jq -r .x'` reads `sh` and passes, and `node bin/orbit.js status --frobnicate` reads `node` and passes, while the orbit sweep never extracts it. The retired tool-set limit named that last member (`node bin/orbit.js`), and the new limit drops it. Either name the class in the inventory's Residual kind, or read past the wrapper.

recommendation_options.label: A
recommendation_options.body: Add to the Residual kind: a tool run as an argument of a declared head (`command <tool> …`, `sh -c '<…>'`, `node <script> …`, including `node bin/orbit.js`), with a matching Residual method line.

recommendation_options.label: B
recommendation_options.body: Close the `command` case by rule: when the head is `command` and the next token is not `-v`/`-V`/`-p`, the head is that next token. Name `sh -c` and `node <script>` in the Residual kind.

findings.reproduction: tokenize('command jq -r .x') from test/helpers/surface-snippets.ts returns segments [["command","jq","-r",".x"]]; by D5 the head is `command`, which the inventory block declares under `utility`, so the line passes and `jq` is never read. Measured with a throwaway vitest probe, since deleted.

findings.title: The read table says a group's grouping is stripped, but the tokenizer strips only a subshell
findings.recommendation: The shared tokenizer strips `(` and `)` only. `{ jq -r .x; }` tokenizes to [["{","jq","-r",".x"],["}"]], so the heads read are `{` and `}`, not `jq`. Shell reserved words and prefixes do the same: `if git diff --quiet; then …; fi` reads `if`, `then` and `fi`; `! git …` reads `!`; `time jq …` reads `time`. None is on today's surface. As written, an implementer could either extend the tokenizer to match the row or leave the row false. And the `utility` kind (utilities, builtins, test words) has no place for a reserved word that a future fence needs declared. Narrow the row to `( … )` and add a row saying that a brace group, reserved word or `!`/`time` prefix is read as the head (and so fails until declared). Then either define where such a head is declared or name it in the residual, since declaring `if` launders whatever follows it, as with the finding on line 54.

findings.title: The stale-table count compares five POSIX rows against twelve heads that include node and sh
findings.recommendation: The baseline table names five POSIX utilities in one row and `node` and `sh` in another, so it names seven of the twelve `utility` heads. The missing five are `rm`, `tail`, `cd`, `[` and `command`. Say 'names seven of the twelve' (design.md:11 and proposal.md:26), or compare like with like.

findings.title: D5 says the inventory catches two members of the places table's residual; it catches one
findings.recommendation: Inside a shell fence the places residual names three members: a `$ ` prompt, an assignment prefix (`VAR=1 orbit …`) and a trailing `\`. The inventory fails only the `$ ` prompt (head `$`). It skips the assignment by design, and then reads the recorded `orbit`, so `VAR=1 orbit --frobnicate` passes both checks. The path-prefixed head D5 also cites belonged to the retired tool-set limit, not to the places table. Restate the claim as one places member plus one retired tool-set member.

findings.title: Two consecutive blank lines where the tool-set table was removed
findings.recommendation: Collapse lines 118-119 to one blank line so the MODIFIED block reads as the baseline did.

commentary: I probed the mechanism rather than reading it. A throwaway vitest file reimplemented the ADDED read table over generatedSurfaces() and the shared tokenize(). It read exactly the twelve utility heads, the `<argv[0]>` placeholder and the four prose heads the block declares. No head was undeclared, every declared head was used, and no flagged inline span starting with a lowercase word was refused. So the day-one exactness claim holds, and Case 2 reproduces. The D2 reader's requirement-level holder test is stricter than its canonical-examples precedent, which checks the capability only. That is deliberate and correct, because another change could modify the sibling orbit-snippet requirement. Both warnings are about the edge of the BOUNDED rule, not its core. The head production is first-token-after-assignments, so any head that runs another command (`command`, `sh -c`, `node`, a reserved word) hides what it runs. The limit should say so, because the exemption list now contains three such heads.

direction.reasoning: The mechanism is measured and holds on today's surface: the exemption block is exact both ways, and the head walk reuses the extractor's own parse instead of a second grammar. What remains is accounting. The named limit omits a class that the declared exemptions themselves open (a wrapper head runs an unread tool), and one read-table row claims tokenizer behaviour that does not exist. Both are text repairs in the delta and should be walked before apply. Neither calls for new mechanism.
